title: Explosive Drone at German Airport and Bulgaria Blast Raise NATO Security Alarm
excerpt: An armed drone found near Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport and a separate explosion in Bulgarian airspace expose growing vulnerabilities in Europe's defence against unmanned aerial threats.
body:
• An explosive-laden drone was discovered near Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 5, prompting a federal terrorism investigation in Germany.
  • A separate drone, identified as a Ukrainian-type Maya decoy, exploded in a Bulgarian sunflower field on August 8, just 1,000 metres from a Trans-Balkan gas pipeline compressor station.
  • Two more drones were spotted over a German military base housing U.S. Patriot air defence maintenance facilities two days after the Leipzig incident.
  • Russia dismissed the Leipzig attack as a "fabricated provocation," while NATO allies debate whether Europe is ready to counter the mounting drone threat.

Armed Drone Found at Major NATO Logistics Hub

Airport workers discovered a drone equipped with explosives and a detonator late on Tuesday, August 5, near a runway at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, according to German federal prosecutors. The device was found in the immediate vicinity of several Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo aircraft, which have used the airport as an operating base since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

https://x.com/SprinterPress/status/2086158113661452624

The southern runway was closed while explosives experts examined the drone and removed its detonator. A confidential German police report found the explosives were of "high military grade," according to Süddeutsche Zeitung.

"Such threat situations are not carried out by amateurs, but must be prepared very professionally and executed professionally."

— Alexander Dobrindt, German Interior Minister

In a possibly linked incident, a DHL cargo plane performing a go-around due to the runway closure struck what prosecutors believe was a second drone. The jet sustained slight damage and was diverted to Hanover. German investigators suspect the second object may have been a surveillance drone, possibly carrying a camera to record an attack, Bild newspaper reported.

Anti-extremism prosecutors and counterterrorism officers have taken over the investigation, characterising the incident as "a serious attack on the transportation and logistics infrastructure in Germany" that posed a threat to both external and internal security.

Drone Explodes Near Bulgarian Gas Pipeline

Three days later, on Saturday, August 8, a drone entered Bulgarian airspace from Romania and exploded near the village of Kardam, close to the Romanian border. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said there were no casualties or infrastructure damage.

The explosion site was 1,000 metres from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, which stretches from Turkey to Ukraine, and just 200 metres from Romania's compressor station.

Bulgaria's defence ministry identified the drone as most likely a Maya decoy drone, a type widely used by the Ukrainian armed forces. The ministry said there was no reason to believe the incident was intentional. Ukraine has not commented on the Bulgarian incident.

Radev noted that the drone was not detected in either Bulgarian or Romanian airspace before the explosion, underscoring the challenge of identifying small unmanned aerial vehicles. He flagged delays in the delivery of high-precision radars to the Bulgarian army and pledged action to strengthen surveillance along the border.

Pattern of Escalating Drone Threats Across Europe

Two days after the Leipzig incident, on Thursday, August 7, two more drones were spotted above a military base in Mechernich in the western German state of North Rhine-Westphalia, roughly 35 kilometres from the Belgian border. German media reported that the Bundeswehr site houses a high-security underground storage facility and serves as a maintenance base for U.S. Patriot air defence systems.

The episodes fit into a broader pattern of unauthorised drone activity that has alarmed European security agencies. German airports have been on heightened alert following overflights at military facilities, energy terminals, seaports, and logistics companies. Federal police have said the overflights could have been organised by Russian agents. In other parts of Europe, drones near airports have halted flights, NATO airspace has been violated in Poland and Romania, and underwater cables have been disrupted in the Baltic Sea.

Charlie Edwards, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said the armed drone at Leipzig represented a departure from espionage or disruption. "A UAV carrying a charge with a detonator that failed is a different proposition, and it is likely, though not yet certain, that this was intended to function rather than to be found," he said.

Russia Denies Involvement

The Russian embassy in Berlin dismissed the Leipzig event as a "fabricated provocation" in a statement published on Friday. "It is obvious that this hastily fabricated provocation only serves the interests of Kyiv and the militarist wing of the European political class," the embassy said.

German government officials have not publicly blamed any foreign country for the incidents, but several lawmakers have pointed to Russia. Moscow has denied involvement in similar drone incidents and in a 2024 series of incendiary devices found in air cargo shipments at the same Leipzig DHL warehouse.

What's Next

The incidents are likely to intensify calls within NATO for member states to invest in counter-drone capabilities. Leipzig/Halle Airport plays a significant role in supplying Ukraine through NATO's Strategic Airlift International Solution programme, which uses Antonov aircraft based there to transport weapons and heavy equipment. The investigation into the armed drone's origin, range, and launch site is ongoing, with analysis of the device expected to yield critical clues.
